item.title: Who Am I Without the Mask?
item.description:
Masking

Who Am I Without the Mask?

Discovering your identity after decades of camouflaging.

Posted July 5, 2026

Key points
  • Autistic people often find it difficult to know who they are after years of camouflaging.
  • Camouflaging usually begins in childhood and can shape identity over a lifetime.
  • You don't need to reject every part of your camouflaged self to live more authentically.

“I don’t know who I am.” This is what Anisha told me after confirming she was autistic. It’s something I hear regularly, often after the relief that comes following a diagnosis has settled. The reason it’s such an intrinsic part of so many autistic women’s experience is because of the camouflaging that many of us rely on. Camouflaging is more than simply having a “professional” self and a “private” self, which is something most people can identify with. For many people, it’s a complete suppression of who they really are from a very early age.

Camouflaging shows up in different ways, one of which is hiding feelings of discomfort. My first memories of doing this were in primary school, where I experienced extremely high levels of anxiety from the first day I started. I worried about spelling something incorrectly, getting the answer to a sum wrong, being late, or having to speak in class. By my second year, I was terrified of being bullied, and my biggest worry, the one that dominated my weeks and led to severe migraines, was PE.

The joy of discovering your identity after camouflaging.
Source: Sunny Studio/Canva

The only relief I had from this constant anxiety was when I had a migraine and could spend the day locked in the dark. But apart from that obvious sign that something wasn’t quite right, nobody knew about the permanent heightened state of anxiety I was in, because I hid it. I hid behaviours that had been open and natural before starting school, including sucking my thumb. I was horrified by other children who still sucked their thumbs in class. Even when I was 5, I had such strong camouflaging instincts that I hid any behaviour I thought was inappropriate.

These are just a few examples of how, from a very early age, autistic children often become aware of having to be someone else around other people. Camouflaging isn’t something we suddenly learn in adulthood as social situations become more complex. It’s something many of us have been doing our whole lives. And because these behaviours become so ingrained, by adulthood they often leave us asking, “Who am I?”

Can You Find the "Real You” After Years of Camouflaging?

When you’ve spent a lifetime monitoring your facial expressions, rehearsing conversations, suppressing stims, forcing eye contact, and making decisions based on what other people expect rather than what feels natural to you, it can be difficult to know which parts of you were chosen freely and which were shaped by necessity. That can feel incredibly disorientating.

article continues after advertisement

There’s a temptation to try to find “the real you,” the person underneath the mask. But approaching identity with that goal in mind is rarely helpful. Identity is complex. Who you are today has been shaped by your experiences, including camouflaging. Whilst there may have been a more fundamental version of you in very early childhood, that version no longer exists.

“I wonder if I’d have been very different if I hadn’t camouflaged quite as much as I did,” Paula told me. As she reflected on her life, she realised how often she had agreed with people because she’d been told she was “too blunt,” and how private she had become because she worried she was “weird.” “Nobody really knows the real me,” she said, and that realisation brought a great deal of sadness. But part of our work together was recognising that the person she had become had also been shaped by a lifetime of camouflaging.

Would she have been different if she hadn’t camouflaged as much as she did? The short answer is yes. But it’s impossible to separate who we are from the experiences that have shaped us, and camouflaging is one of those experiences. As autistic women who have spent a lifetime camouflaging, what we can do is acknowledge how it has influenced our identity. We can also recognise some of its positive aspects, whether that’s learning to respond to people in a softer way or hiding our extreme boredom during a conversation. Most of us have complex lives and complex identities, and camouflaging simply becomes part of that complexity.

If, like Anisha and Paula, you’re struggling with who you are after discovering you’re autistic, it’s important not to think of all camouflaging as bad or to feel you need to eliminate the camouflaged version of yourself in pursuit of something more “authentic.” That can create a great deal of self-judgement and place unnecessary pressure on you to change everything at once. Instead, approach this journey with curiosity rather than urgency.

How Do You Start Embracing Your Identity?

What’s one thing you’re curious about? Sometimes starting with a small physical change can be surprisingly powerful. Some of my clients have spent years suppressing their personality by wearing clothes or decorating their homes in ways that were designed to fit in rather than reflect their tastes. Is there something you could gently experiment with?

article continues after advertisement

Or perhaps camouflaging shows up in the social situations you repeatedly force yourself to attend despite finding them exhausting. Rather than feeling you have to say no to everything overnight, ask yourself where your identity feels most forced. Where is it hardest to be yourself? What message would you be sending yourself if you said no to just one thing over the next week or two? How might that single act begin to strengthen your sense of identity and reinforce the belief that your needs matter too?

I've had well over five years now to consider what identity means on a personal level, and at this midlife point I can honestly say that I feel like myself when I'm around other people. Part of that is embracing what other people might see as my "bossiness," and part of it is being more open about my sometimes unusual sense of humour. I'll never be comfortable sucking my thumb in front of anyone other than my closest family, and that's fine, but I am much more comfortable rocking or swaying during client sessions. As I've become more outwardly open about what makes me "me," my internal sense of identity has grown stronger.

Perhaps that's what discovering your identity after decades of camouflaging really looks like. Not becoming someone new, but gradually giving yourself permission to be the person you've been all along.

item.title: Some People Are the Last to Know How They're Being Perceived
item.description:
Relationships

Some People Are the Last to Know How They're Being Perceived

We live inside the story of ourselves. Others don't.

Posted July 5, 2026

What can we do or say when our partner or someone we love is completely unaware of how they come across to others in the world, and yet is continually frustrated about other people’s responses to them? How do we make things better when someone we care about can’t see their own behavior accurately, when they have a skewed version of themselves, and are certain they’re not doing what they’re actually doing? Is it possible to move the dial forward when someone rejects and feels victimized by the feedback and results they keep getting from the world on account of that behavior?

Risa’s kids frequently complain to her about her husband, their father. All three of her children tell her that he’s constantly shouting at them, telling them what they’re doing wrong, and instructing them on what they need to do to change—hammering at them with the same message over and over again. They tell her that he doesn’t listen or ask questions about why they make the choices they make; he barrages them with criticism, which he says is “advice and guidance.” Each child has said the same thing, and indeed, Risa has witnessed this exact behavior, this relentlessness and aggression from her husband, again and again.

Perception Versus Reality

Recently, her husband recounted an interaction with one of their children. As he described what he'd said to their child, he became agitated and angry, raising his voice to nearly a shout. After listening for a while, Risa gently asked him whether the tone he used in describing the interaction was the same as the tone used when delivering the message to their child. Risa had been in this situation many times, listening to his report on an interaction while having witnessed something very different than what he described. Her husband became even angrier after her question and insisted that, of course, he had not spoken to the girl that way; he knew better than that. He had, of course, lovingly and patiently presented his points, just as he always did to their kids. He knew how to be a dad, and she was implying that he was unaware and blind to the situation. Then he went after Risa—for judging him and claiming to know him better than he knew himself.

Interactions like this left Risa between a rock and a hard place. She loved her husband and also knew exactly how he sounded when he was trying to make a point, share his wisdom, and offer guidance. For years, she had watched him go after their kids hard, speak aggressively, and be critical even while he thought he was being helpful. She’d experienced him that way as long as she'd known him, the same way her kids experienced him.

Risa had lovingly tried to suggest to her husband that the way he thought he was speaking to their kids might not match what he sounded like when he was speaking to them. And, that it might be a good idea to pay attention to the feedback that he consistently received from everyone in the family, the responses that were repeated over and over. She’d reminded him that they were all on his side—not criticizing him, not shaming him—and that the kids were trying to share their experience of him, how he came across. In as many non-threatening, non-wounding, non-shaming ways as she could come up with, while always pointing out that she knew his intentions were loving, Risa had tried to convey that the way their kids actually experienced their father in reality was as someone unhelpful and critical (which were very softened versions of what the kids had actually expressed).

But no matter what she tried, her husband insisted that he was communicating the way he imagined he was communicating, and behaving the way he thought he was behaving. His narrative on who he was didn’t align with reality, at least when it came to his behavior. No matter what response he received from the people he loved, he vehemently denied any suggestion that he was anything other than the character he’d written for himself in his own self-story, who he’d decided he was. His identity in his narrative: He was aware of his own behavior, and also a wise and loving dad. And nothing, not even reality, was going to change that.

article continues after advertisement

The Need to Protect Self-Image

You could say that Risa’s husband was delusional and out of touch with reality; the truth is, he was just a normal human being—living the way most people live—in their own story of reality, their own story about themselves, their own narrative of who and how they are. He trusted that what he believed, what he needed to believe to feel good about himself, was truly happening. The movie playing in his head, in his private cinema, was real. The narrative her husband had written about the kind of “dad” and “conscious” human he was, which he continually pointed out, needed to be upheld no matter what reality dictated. Any suggestion that something else might be true (at times) had the potential to destabilize him.

Ultimately, any kink in the armor that protected his self-narrative, his sense of self, threatened to unleash a deep and underlying shame and sense of not-enoughness that he’d carried since childhood. Allowing the reality of his kids’ experience of him brought him into direct contact with his own fear that he might actually be like his own dad—an emotional bully. Any suggestion that he could be experienced as something other than who he was in his own narrative had to be thoroughly rejected.

In Part 2 of this series, I’ll suggest options for dealing with someone who’s behaving in a way they don’t think they’re behaving, and at the same time, when they won’t let in the reality of other people’s experience—of them. I’ll offer a way to move the situation forward when the process seems stuck—a soft place to land between your rock and hard place.

item.title: When Your Adult Child Blames You for Their Struggles
item.description:
Guilt

When Your Adult Child Blames You for Their Struggles

Parents can respond with empathy, boundaries, and less guilt-driven rescuing.

Posted July 5, 2026

Key points
  • Validate pain without accepting all the blame.
  • Know when helping turns into rescuing.
  • Set calm, healthy boundaries that support connection and growth.

Over the last 35 years as a psychologist, I have coached many parents of struggling adult children and worked with many adult children as well. Based on my experience, parents of struggling adult children often live with a quietly painful question: How much of this is my fault? If your adult child is anxious, depressed, unmotivated, financially dependent, angry, stuck, or in near-constant crisis episodes, it can be hard not to look backward. Maybe your adult child has implied you're the one responsible for their hardships and struggles. Or, maybe there is no implication because they straight-up tell you. They say that your parenting, your marriage, your blind spots, your lack of listening, or your mistakes are the reason they are suffering now.

A Powerful Mix of Sadness, Guilt, Defensiveness, and Fear

Parents share with me that they experience almost every imaginable emotion when their adult children are in pain. If you can relate, then perhaps you have found yourself overexplaining, apologizing, sending money, solving problems, or tolerating disrespect because part of you worries that if you don't, then you'll be abandoning them. I get it. But please ask yourself if guilt and other painful emotions have usually been a healthy guide to helping your adult child?

The challenge for many families is not simply that an adult child is in pain. It's that the family begins organizing itself around that pain in ways that don't promote growth. Parents become consumed with avoiding conflict or reducing their child's short-term distress. Adult children may become more focused on what happened to them than on what they can do now. I have seen compassion far too many times turn not only into compassion fatigue but also into overfunctioning, with support turning into rescuing.

Managing Your Guilt and Other Emotions Is Key

I wrote my new book, You Ruined My Life—Now You Owe Me, as a distillation of my many years of hearing the heart-wrenching stories of parents who want to help but also feel drained by blame, conflict, and the pressure to keep rescuing. Many adult children have also opened up to me about their pain, and I'd like to share three reminders from my reflections and consequent writing to please keep in mind.

First, you can validate pain without accepting all the blame. Being empathetic does not mean losing yourself.
My second caution for you is to watch for when support turns into rescuing. If your help repeatedly shields your adult child from discomfort, responsibility, or consequences, it may be relieving short-term distress while prolonging long-term stuckness.
My final piece of advice is to replace your guilt-driven reactions with calm, loving boundaries.

Parents are most often helpful when they stop overprotecting, communicate with steadiness, and hold limits that support responsibility rather than dependence.

item.title: How to Help Children Through Divorce and Build Resilience
item.description:
Divorce

How to Help Children Through Divorce and Build Resilience

What every parent can do to help children thrive during and after divorce.

Posted July 5, 2026

Key points
  • Children need loving, supportive, and emotionally responsive parents—not perfect ones—to thrive after divorce.
  • Consistency and reassurance build resilience during family transitions.
  • Healthy co-parenting supports children's well-being and long-term adjustment.

When parents decide to divorce, one question often overshadows every other concern: "How will this affect my children?" This is a question born out of love—and often, a tremendous amount of guilt.

While divorce is undeniably a significant life transition, research offers an encouraging message: it isn't the divorce itself that most strongly predicts a child's long-term emotional well-being. What matters most is the environment children experience before, during, and after separation. Children who continue to feel loved, protected, and emotionally secure can adapt remarkably well, even during difficult circumstances.

Although every situation is unique, the children who adjust most successfully often have one thing in common: the adults in their lives prioritize the children's physical, mental, and emotional needs over their own conflicts.

Start with Honesty—and Reassurance

One of the hardest conversations parents will ever have is telling their children about a divorce. Whenever it is emotionally and physically safe to do so, both parents should consider sharing the news. This sends an important message that, although the marriage is ending, the parenting relationship continues.

Children of every age need to hear the same reassuring messages repeatedly:

  • This is not your fault.
  • We both love you.
  • We will always be your parents.
  • You will continue to be cared for.
  • You never have to choose between us.

Children don't need to know the details of marital conflict, financial disagreements, or whether infidelity was involved. Those are adult problems that children may not be emotionally equipped to carry. Instead, they need simple, age-appropriate explanations and confidence that the adults are taking care of the situation.

Children Experience Divorce Differently at Different Ages

Understanding how children process divorce can help parents respond with empathy rather than frustration.

Toddlers and Preschoolers

Young children don't fully understand what divorce means. Instead, they notice changes in routines and a parent's absence. Their biggest concern is often whether the people they depend on will continue to love and care for them.

article continues after advertisement

Parents may notice increased clinginess, sleep disruptions, tantrums, separation anxiety, or even temporary developmental regressions, such as toileting accidents or thumb-sucking. These behaviors aren't signs of manipulation—they're signs that a young child's nervous system is struggling with uncertainty.

Predictable routines, consistent transitions between homes, and repeated reassurance that both parents love them provide the emotional stability young children need.

School-Aged Children

Elementary-aged children have a better understanding of divorce. Yet younger school-aged children often engage in what psychologists call "magical thinking." This is when a child erroneously believes that their thoughts, words, or actions cause a change in the world around them. Even children who never say these thoughts aloud may quietly carry feelings of guilt.

Parents should repeatedly reassure them that divorce is an adult decision and that nothing the child did—or could have done—caused it.

Children of this age also benefit from being encouraged to talk about their feelings without worrying about protecting their parents. Open-ended questions help. "What's been the hardest part for you?" These invite more meaningful conversations than simply asking, "Are you okay?"

Teenagers

Teenagers understand the complexities of relationships more fully, but that doesn't make divorce easier. Some become withdrawn. Others appear angry or emotionally distant. Still others seem unaffected on the surface while quietly grieving significant changes within the family.

One common mistake that parents make is leaning too heavily on teenagers for emotional support. While older children may seem mature, they should never become a parent's therapist, confidant, or messenger between households. Adolescents still need the freedom to be teenagers, not emotional caretakers.

article continues after advertisement

The Power of Healthy Co-Parenting

Parents don't have to agree on everything to co-parent successfully. They need to keep their child's emotional well-being at the center of their decisions.

Healthy co-parenting means communicating directly with one another rather than through the child. It means avoiding criticism of the other parent and resisting the urge to ask children to report on what happens in the other home. Healthy co-parenting involves consistency, collaboration, and a child-centered focus.

While two households won't be identical, maintaining similar expectations around homework, bedtime, screen time, and discipline helps children feel more secure as they move between homes. Parents can avoid comparisons: “Well, in my house__.” Or, “Her dad never__.” This causes division in an already divisive situation.

Understanding Custody Beyond the Schedule

Many parents focus on where children will spend their time, but custody involves more than parenting schedules.

Physical custody refers to where a child lives and how parenting time is divided. Legal custody refers to who has the authority to make major decisions regarding healthcare, education, and other important aspects of a child's life.

In many families, parents share legal custody, meaning they continue making significant decisions together even if the child lives primarily with one parent. Understanding these responsibilities—and communicating respectfully about medical care, school concerns, and mental health treatment—helps reduce confusion and ensures children receive consistent support.

Because custody laws vary by state, parents should work closely with qualified family law professionals to understand their specific rights and responsibilities.

Remember What Children Need Most

Divorce changes the structure of a family, but it doesn't have to diminish the love within it.

Children are remarkably resilient when they know they are safe, deeply loved, and free to maintain healthy relationships with both parents whenever possible. Parents don't have to navigate divorce perfectly. They can remain emotionally available, provide consistent reassurance, and protect children from adult conflict.

article continues after advertisement

Years from now, children are unlikely to remember every custody exchange or holiday schedule. What they are far more likely to remember is whether they felt secure, heard, and unconditionally loved.

And that may become one of the greatest gifts a parent can offer during one of life's most difficult transitions.

item.title: Don’t Wear Mascara to Therapy and Other Tips
item.description:
Therapy

Don’t Wear Mascara to Therapy and Other Tips

Six tips for approaching therapy effectively.

Posted July 5, 2026

Key points
  • In therapy, you control the pace and topics; the therapist offers guidance, not commands.
  • Being raw and honest in sessions speeds up progress—there's no need to hide emotions or imperfections.
  • Growth requires discomfort and patience; change blooms when you leave your comfort zone.

Choosing to engage in therapy is a brave and vulnerable step. Stigma related to mental health issues is decreasing, and getting help has become easier for many individuals than in past generations for a multitude of reasons. However, the process can still be daunting for some.

Here are six tips, including a metaphor for easy visualization and a brief client case example for illustrative context.

Source: Annie Spratt/Unsplash

The Therapist Has a Map, But You Decide the Roads You Will Travel

An anxious new client expressed interest in working on certain aspects of his self-care difficulties, such as his overuse of alcohol, but indicated he was not interested in addressing other domains, such as disordered eating patterns. While a therapist is interested in helping someone live their best life and has specialized training to address various concerns, the client ultimately remains in charge of the process. A therapist can point out significant intersections and suggest experiments with certain paths on the “map” of treatment, but clients choose whether, when, and how quickly things proceed. This client eventually agreed to work on other dysregulated self-care patterns but needed time to build more buy-in.

Therapy Tip: The therapist does not know every pathway or all the answers, but therapists know the significant landmarks and general recommended directions. There are no tricks or traps, just an offering of options that may be helpful to consider.

Source: Katerina/Unsplash

Don’t Wear Mascara to Sessions

There was a kind and complicated woman with whom I worked; she often wore mascara to sessions at the beginning of our work together, only to be chagrinned that black streaks ran down her cheeks halfway through sessions due to her tears. She ultimately chose to stop putting on makeup before her sessions; this represented not only her anticipation of possible emotions that might arise but, even more importantly, an eventual awareness that she didn’t need to attempt to be “put together” for our sessions. She came to value and even embrace the genuine, raw, take-me-as-I-am type of energy she eventually settled and prospered in various domains of her life.

Therapy Tip: The best results are achieved in therapy when someone presents as openly and genuinely as possible. There is no need to cover up anything; nothing is TMI (too much information), and being more real will allow the work to progress faster.

Source: Messala Ciulla/Pexels

First Drafts Are Welcome

A young adult came to therapy to address low energy and motivational issues, but seemed to be concerned that he needed to present in a certain way and tread carefully for fear of being faulted or seen as less competent. While there were certainly family-of-origin patterns that had set the stage for this way of interacting, we did have to come to the understanding that his “first draft” thoughts and idea brainstorming were all fully welcome. Therapy is not a job interview or a test; it is a way to connect with a trained individual around issues of concern and importance.

Therapy Tip: Therapists don’t need clients to have it all figured out, eloquently articulated, or perfectly organized. Part of the treatment is figuring out the words, ideas, and plans together.

Be Prepared for Some Archery

Source: Kampus Pexels

One high-powered, perfectionist client came to therapy interested in changing aspects of her interpersonal relationships as quickly as possible, but was initially resistant to examining past patterns and contributing factors in her history that made closer relationships more challenging. Eventually, we used the metaphor of the arrow, which made sense to her: for someone aiming to shoot an arrow at a target, you pull the arrow back before letting go. She also had to figure out how to aim the arrow at the next behavioral or emotional target. Once she understood the value of making these connections, not to mention increasing her patience for change, she was able to make some significant progress in altering how she interacted with others.

Therapy Tip: Therapists have different theoretical orientations, and different problems will influence how much exploration of the past is needed. No matter what, reflection can be a helpful way to target personal goals more effectively for the future.

We Can Still See Through Windows When They Are Smudgy

Source: Vitya Lapatey/Unsplash

A teenager was referred to therapy by their parents and made it clear from the outset that they weren’t interested in participating. The teen said that things were fine at school, home, and with friends, and they were adamant that nothing needed therapeutic attention. But like a windshield which appears basically functional yet dirties a rag when wiped down, there were some significant symptoms of sadness and anxiety which were indeed interfering with daily functioning. “Cleaning the glass” allowed this teen to improve functioning and live with much more clarity of positive purpose.

Therapy Tip: We sometimes don’t know how much better it can be because our perspective is all we know in the moment. Humans have the capacity to go beyond just surviving and experience a thriving life, and therapy can help.

A Flower Bulb Pushing Through Earth

Parents presented to therapy in hopes of addressing some behavioral issues for their child that had escalated considerably, and we soon uncovered that some household patterns needed shifting. We uncovered how the very well-meaning parents had worked to create a happy, easy life for the child, but also had inadvertently created a child unfamiliar with boundaries, limits, or expectations for contribution. It was not easy for all the family members to make changes to their routines, and it required a fair amount of discomfort; however, they became happier and eventually functioned in a healthier way. Like a bulb planted in the earth, the tightly coiled bulb must push against the ground's resistance to bloom.

Source: Jaroslaw Ponikowski/Pexels

Therapy Tip: Growth and change are not always easy, smooth, or fast; however, moving beyond one’s comfort zone to bloom is exactly where change begins. This is neuroplasticity, the brain’s capacity for change.

item.title: 7 False Beliefs That Keep You From Real Closeness
item.description:
Child Development

7 False Beliefs That Keep You From Real Closeness

Why the beliefs that feel protective are the ones holding you back.

Posted July 5, 2026

Key points
  • If you grew up emotionally neglected, you may carry quiet beliefs that keep you from closeness.
  • These beliefs make sharing your feelings seem like a burden, a weakness, or a risk.
  • Every one of them is false; sharing your feelings actually draws people closer.
  • You learned these beliefs as a child, which means you can also unlearn them now.
Source: Cavan for Adobe/StockAdobe

You keep your worries to yourself. You smooth over conflict instead of facing it. When a friend asks how you are, you say you’re fine, even when you are not. None of this feels like a choice; it feels like simply how you are.

As a psychologist who has specialized in childhood emotional neglect for decades, I have come to recognize this pattern and the quiet beliefs underneath it in many warm and capable people. Here are seven of those beliefs. As you read them, put a mental check mark next to any that feel true to you.

  • Sharing your feelings with others will make you look weak.
  • It's best not to fight if you want to have a good relationship.
  • Sharing your feelings or troubles with another person burdens them.
  • Talking about a problem isn't helpful. Only action solves a problem.
  • Sharing your feelings or troubles with another person will chase them away.
  • Letting others see your weaknesses puts you at a disadvantage.
  • If you let other people see how you feel, they will use it against you.

As you read the list of beliefs above, did any jump out at you? Was there one, or two, or more, that you thought, "Hey, that one's not false!"?

If so, you are not alone. Many people go through their lives following some or all of these guidelines, and these rules can hold a person back. These beliefs have the power to keep you emotionally distant from others, damage your friendships and marriage, and leave you feeling alone in the world.

The beliefs are typically rooted in your childhood. They are often messages passed down from one generation to another. They take root in your mind and live there, sometimes outside of your awareness.

How Childhood Emotional Neglect Teaches You the False Beliefs

These ideas tend to thrive in any family that struggles with emotions, either by over- or under-expressing them. They're so common among folks who grew up with childhood emotional neglect that they're included in my book, Running on Empty. All of the beliefs are based on false notions of how emotions work.

Childhood emotional neglect is not about what your parents did to you. It’s about what did not happen: the absence of having your emotional needs noticed and validated by others. Most emotionally neglectful parents are doing their best, and many were raised in the very same way. It’s often no one's fault. But when you grow up this way, you learn to treat your own feelings as a problem, and these beliefs are some of the lessons you carry out the door and into adulthood.

If you grew up in a family that didn't understand how to manage, express, or talk about emotion, you probably didn't learn how or when to share or be vulnerable. You may have learned that it's actually wrong to communicate about these things.

And there’s a good chance that some of the seven beliefs were communicated to you, either directly or indirectly.

The 7 False Beliefs Made True

  1. Letting people see your feelings usually makes them like you more. It also fosters intimacy.
  2. The hallmark of a strong, healthy relationship or friendship is the ability to have conflict, process it together, and work through it together. Fighting is often a sign of closeness.
  3. Sharing your feelings or troubles with the right person at the right time does not burden them. It increases warmth and caring from the other person.
  4. Talking about a problem with a well-chosen person can help you with your perspective, feel less burdened, sort out your feelings and thoughts, and sometimes even find solutions.
  5. Sharing your feelings or troubles with the right person will help them feel closer to you.
  6. Letting another person see your weakness does not put you at a disadvantage unless the other person is the type to take advantage of you. Be aware of who you're letting in. The huge majority of people will not take advantage.
  7. If you let someone see how you feel, they will know and understand you better, and that's a good thing. The only exception is if they are actively trying to hurt you. Generally, if there are people like this in your life, you know who they are. Do not share with them.

How to Change Your Beliefs From False to True

  • Choose your people carefully. Who you open your heart to matters, whether a friend or lover. Focus on integrity, trust, and care. Pay attention to the other person's intentions. None of the true beliefs apply if the person is not trustworthy.
  • Timing is everything. We all underestimate the importance of timing. Choose your moment, taking into account the other person's mood, needs, and situation. The same message can have a very different impact at the wrong time versus the right one.
  • Take chances. There is no intimacy without vulnerability. To change these beliefs, you will have to put yourself in uncomfortable situations.
  • The Costanza Experiment. Remember the Seinfeld episode when George decided to go through an entire week doing the opposite of what he would normally do? (If you're under 40, you may not have seen it, but the concept will still work for you.) This would mean doing the opposite of what you normally do when it comes to sharing your feelings. Tell your friend about your work worries instead of keeping them to yourself. Share your financial stress with your brother instead of pretending everything's fine. Fight it out with your spouse instead of avoiding the conflict.

Take a chance, and see what happens. The false beliefs will begin to melt away as you experience the value of trust, openness, and closeness. Your relationships will thrive, and a whole new world will open up to you.

A version of this post also appears on emotionalneglect.com
